title: Q3 Board Update

summary.overview: Hannah presented the Q3 update to the board. Revenue reached 2.4 million dollars in annualized recurring revenue, up 18 percent quarter over quarter, with net revenue retention at 112 percent. Aisha reported 19 months of runway at the current burn after a higher-than-planned cloud bill, and proposed cost controls on transcription spend. Jordan outlined the Q4 roadmap focused on search, integrations, and enterprise security. Nora asked for a clearer view of customer concentration and pushed for a hiring plan tied to milestones. The board approved two additional engineering hires contingent on Q4 pipeline targets.

action_items.text: Circulate the full Q3 financial pack and the customer concentration breakdown to the board
Present a transcription cost reduction plan with a target for gross margin
Share the detailed Q4 roadmap with milestones and success metrics
Draft the milestone-linked hiring plan for the two approved engineering roles
Introduce Hannah to two potential enterprise design partners

transcript.summary: Hannah summarized Q3 growth, retention, and customer wins.

transcript: Good morning, everyone, and thank you, Nora, for making the time. I'll walk through the quarter in four parts: the business highlights, the financials from Aisha, product and roadmap from Jordan, and then the decisions we'd like the board's input on.
Sounds good. I've read the pre-read, so feel free to focus on what's changed and what worries you rather than repeating the numbers I've seen.

Perfect. The headline is that we ended the quarter at two point four million dollars in annualized recurring revenue, which is up eighteen percent from last quarter. That's slightly ahead of the sixteen percent we planned.
That's good. What drove the beat? Was it new customers or expansion?

Mostly expansion. Net revenue retention came in at one hundred twelve percent, which is the best we've had. Existing customers added seats after their pilots, particularly in healthcare and logistics.
The logistics deals were largely inbound after we published the case study in July, so that content paid for itself within two months.
What about new logos? I'd like to know whether growth is coming from a healthy mix or whether we're leaning on a few accounts.
Fourteen new customers this quarter against nine last quarter. Aisha has the concentration breakdown in the financial section, so I'll hand over to her.

transcript.summary: ARR, burn, runway, and the cloud cost overrun.

transcript: Thanks, Hannah. Quick summary of the financials. Revenue for the quarter was six hundred ten thousand dollars, in line with plan. Gross margin was sixty-eight percent, which is lower than the seventy-two we projected.
That's the number I wanted to ask about. What's behind the margin gap?
Almost entirely cloud and transcription costs. Usage grew faster than we expected, and we're paying per audio minute for transcription. That line is about thirty percent higher than budget.
Is that sustainable? If usage keeps growing and margin keeps shrinking, that changes the story we tell investors.

That's the right concern. We have three levers. Negotiate volume pricing with our transcription vendor, process some audio with a cheaper model for lower-priority meetings, and optimize how we store recordings, which is a hidden cost.

I can speak to the second one. We've tested a lighter-weight model on internal meetings, and quality was within a couple of points for clear audio. We'd keep the premium model for customer-facing calls where accuracy matters most.
I'd want to see a specific target, not just levers. What gross margin do you think is achievable and by when?
My estimate is back to seventy percent by the end of Q1 and seventy-three by mid-year. I'll put together a proper plan with the savings for each lever so you can challenge the assumptions.
Good. That's what I want to see.

On cash, we ended the quarter with four point one million in the bank. Net burn was two hundred ten thousand a month, which gives us nineteen months of runway. That's down from twenty-two last quarter, mostly because of the margin issue and two hires we made early.
Nineteen months is okay but I'd want to be fundraising with at least twelve in hand. Does your plan assume we raise in the second half of next year?
Yes, that's the working assumption. We'd start conversations in Q2 if the metrics keep trending the way they are.
Understood. And customer concentration? Aisha, is anyone more than ten percent of revenue?

One customer is eleven percent, and the top five are about thirty-four percent together. I'll circulate the full breakdown with the financial pack after this meeting so you can see names and contract renewal dates.

transcript.summary: Q4 roadmap priorities: search, integrations, and enterprise readiness.

transcript: Great. Jordan, can you take us through product?
Sure. Three themes for Q4. First, search across all meetings, which customers have asked for in nearly every interview. We're in the middle of building it and expect a beta in about three weeks.
Is it a differentiator or table stakes? I'm trying to understand how it affects retention.

Honestly it's closer to table stakes now, but it directly addresses the number one churn reason we've seen, which is that people lose track of past meetings. We expect it to help retention more than acquisition.

Second theme is integrations. Customers want action items to flow into their ticketing and project tools. We're starting with two integrations, chosen based on demand, and will add more through a public API.
A ticketing system popular with logistics and operations teams and a project management tool used by most of our mid-market customers. Together they cover about half of our pipeline conversations.

The third theme is enterprise readiness. Single sign-on, data residency in the US and EU, and audit logs. Several larger deals are blocked on those, and they're prerequisites for the bigger customers we want to land next year.
How big is the enterprise opportunity versus the risk of distracting the team from the core product?

It's a real trade-off. The work is mostly one-time, about eight weeks for two engineers, and it unlocks deals that are three to five times our average contract. I think it's worth it, but I'll share a detailed plan with milestones so you can see where we'd stop if it gets too expensive.

transcript.summary: Pipeline health, sales hiring, and enterprise design partners.

transcript: On go-to-market, pipeline is two point nine million dollars against a Q4 target of seven hundred fifty thousand in new bookings. That's a healthy coverage ratio of about four to one if the typical conversion holds.
How reliable is that conversion assumption? Sales cycles in enterprise tend to stretch.

Fair challenge. For mid-market, we close in about forty days. For the enterprise deals, we're seeing about ninety days, so some of that pipeline will slip into Q1. I'd say realistically we'll land five hundred thousand of it in Q4.
Our forecast uses five hundred thousand for exactly that reason, so there's no surprise relative to the plan.
Good. What would help you most from me on the go-to-market side?
Introductions to enterprise design partners. We'd like two or three larger companies who would work with us on the security requirements in exchange for pricing and influence on the roadmap.
I know a couple of people at logistics and insurance companies who might be interested. Let me think about who is the best fit and I'll make the introductions in the next week or two.
That would be incredibly helpful. Thank you.

transcript.summary: Board approval of two engineering hires, tied to pipeline milestones.

transcript: Now the decision we'd like input on. We'd like to add two engineers in Q4 to build the enterprise features without slowing down the core roadmap. Cost is about three hundred eighty thousand dollars annually, fully loaded.
Given the margin and runway situation, I'm hesitant to add burn without something tying it to results. Can you link the hiring to milestones?
We could. For example, the first hire starts when the pilot pipeline for enterprise reaches one million dollars, and the second when we sign the first enterprise design partner.
I like that structure. I'd also want to see what happens to runway in each scenario. If both hires happen, you're down to about seventeen months, I think.
Seventeen months, yes, and it recovers somewhat if margin improves as planned. I'll include the scenarios in the financial pack.
I'll draft the hiring plan with the milestones and the scenarios and send it to you for sign-off. We won't open the roles until you've approved the final version.
That works for me. Subject to that plan, the board approves the two roles. Anything else you want us to weigh in on today?
Only that the next meeting is in January and we'll have the margin plan and the first enterprise results by then. Thank you all for the thoughtful questions.
Thank you, Hannah, Aisha, and Jordan. It's a good quarter and I appreciate the candor on the cost side.
I'll send the financial pack within the hour, including the concentration table.
And I'll follow up with the roadmap and milestones by next week. Thanks, everyone.
